title: Singing
hookLine: the one who sings prays twice
tomorrow: what does a priest do after the last Mass on a Sunday night?

cards: At Mass, it's easy to stand with the hymnal open and only mouth the words. Then someone quotes the old line: the one who sings prays twice. The Catechism credits the idea to Saint Augustine.
But Augustine, in his own Confessions, argued with himself about singing in church, and both sides of that argument are still alive in the Church today. So did he really mean it?

teach.h: SIDE ONE: TEARS AT THE HYMNS.
teach.b: Side one. In Milan, newly baptized, Augustine wept at the hymns and songs of the church. The voices flowed into his ears, he writes, and the truth flowed into his heart.
Singing carried him toward God. Side two, later in the same book.
He worries that the sweetness of the music sometimes moves him more than the words being sung, and when it does, he counts it a fault and would rather not hear the singer.
He even weighs the plainer way of Athanasius, who had the psalms read with so little rise and fall of voice it was closer to speaking than singing.

Then, carefully, he leans toward keeping the singing, for the sake of weaker hearts lifted by it. Whether he said prays twice in exactly those words, the sources leave unclear. The Church holds both instincts.
The Second Vatican Council calls its musical tradition a treasure and gives Gregorian chant pride of place, and the same document wants the whole people singing, not only a choir.

teach.h: SIDE TWO: THE TUNE OVER THE WORDS.
teach.b: At its best, side one says: music opens a door that words alone can't.
Side two says: keep the words in front, or the song becomes the point.
Both treat singing as prayer, not decoration.

how: At Mass, Catholics sing hymns, the responsorial psalm, the Gloria, the Holy, Holy and the Amen; some parishes keep Gregorian chant, and a choir or cantor may lead the people.

o: prayer carried on breath and melody, alone or together
a performance by a trained choir for the people
a way to fill the quiet moments during Mass

p: the tune moved him more than the words
psalms closer to speaking than singing

s: the Catechism credits the idea that singing is praying twice to Augustine
it does, though whether he said it in exactly those words is unclear.
Augustine never had doubts about music in church
in the Confessions he worries the music sometimes moves him more than the words.

games.q: your parish debates: a trained choir singing chant, or simple songs everyone can sing. you lean toward everyone. what's the choir side's best case?
o: beautiful, demanding music can open a door words alone can't.
people in the pews would rather sit back and listen anyway.
chant is the only music the Church allows at Mass.
games.why: the Council gives chant pride of place and calls the tradition a treasure, and it also wants the people singing. both are the Church's own instincts.

practice: If you know a hymn, a psalm refrain, or even the sung Amen from Mass, sing or hum one line quietly, as many times as fits.

Don't judge your voice; notice the breath it takes and where you feel it, in your chest, your throat, your face. If singing isn't possible right now, listen to one piece of sacred music instead and let a single line stay with you.

wordCard.voice: Singing. Prayer carried on breath and melody, alone in a car or with a whole church. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: sing to the Lord, the opening of Psalm 95 (96 in most Bibles) in the Vulgate.

carryVoice: The line to keep: sing it, even if it's only a hum from the back pew. Until tomorrow.
